articles.description:
Your AI coding agent has a harness. It has system instructions, tool permissions, validation scripts, automated tests, and guardrails designed to prevent it from doing something stupid.
Your harness needs a feedback loop
Consider a familiar scenario.
You ask an AI coding agent to implement a feature. It modifies a file outside the intended scope. You investigate and add a restriction to prevent the same thing from happening again.
A few days later, the agent makes another out-of-scope change.
You add another instruction.
Then another check.
Eventually, your AGENTS.md, tool configuration, CI pipeline, and validation scripts contain a growing collection of rules intended to prevent past mistakes.
But are these controls actually effective?

articles.description:
By Rokas Remeika. Published 14 October 2026.
Trunk creation APIs generally create resources rather than upserting them. Any provisioning path run twice produces duplicate trunks, leaving your outbound dialer pointing to a stale ID. Separately, raw carrier trunks use an IP allowlist for inbound authenticity. If the carrier's signalling CIDR blocks are missing from that list, inbound INVITEs are dropped before your application exists. To fix both, wrap provisioning in a name-keyed create-or-update script, and pin the exact published carrier CIDRs on the inbound trunk.
You run your infrastructure provisioning script, redeploy your environment, or retry a failed setup step. Shortly after, you open your provider console and see multiple SIP trunks sharing the exact same name but holding entirel…

articles.author: TheEditPDF
articles.description:
Most PDF tools ask for the same trade-off: upload your document to someone else's server, create an account, and hope a paywall does not appear halfway through. That is a problem when the file is a contract, a resume, a medical form, or anything else you would rather not send anywhere.
I built TheEditPDF to remove that trade-off.
It is a collection of 34 free PDF tools that run entirely in your browser. Your files are processed on your device, so nothing is uploaded. There is no signup, nothing to install, and no watermark.
You can edit a PDF, add text, images, links and signatures, merge or split files, compress a large PDF, delete or rotate pages, protect a file with a password, redact sensitive text, and convert between PDF and formats such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, JPG and PNG. It works on a phone, tablet or computer — just open your browser and start.
Try it here: https://theeditpdf.com
If you work with PDFs regularly, I would love to hear which tool you use most, and what would make this more useful for you.
articles.title: I built a free PDF editor that never uploads your files

I've been developing Encryption-tool, an open-source PHP project designed to make file encryption, encrypted package management, and secure data transfer more reliable.

Argon2id for password-based key derivation: Password-derived keys are computationally expensive to guess, making offline password guessing more costly. This raises the cost of attacks but does not eliminate the risk of weak passwords.

articles.author: Gaurav Guha
articles.description:
Supabase gives the browser a key that talks straight to your database. There is no API server in the middle deciding who gets what, which means your Row Level Security (RLS) policies are your application's actual permission layer.
Most tutorials stop at auth.uid() = user_id. Real apps need roles, team tenancy, paid content access, and public pages with private drafts. Here is how RLS works in practice, five common architectural patterns, security mistakes to avoid, and how to test your rules before shipping.
Every request to the Supabase Data API runs as one of three Postgres roles:
anon: No signed-in user. RLS applies.
authenticated: A signed-in user's access token is present. RLS applies.
service_role: Your server, using a secret key. Bypasses RLS.
Postgres runs two checks for each incom…
articles.title: Supabase RLS Explained: Policies, Roles, and Common Security Mistakes
